In a recent development, puppyhood is a huge learning curve â for both owner and dog â and managing a puppyâs energy can be one of the hardest parts of it. Hyperactivity is common, and the good news is that knowing what causes it makes it much easier to help a puppy calm down. The reasons range from ordinary puppy exuberance to, on rare occasions, a health problem.

Puppies burn energy by exploring and playing, but they can run out of things to do. A mix of toys, activities, and walks helps manage their energy. Without it, boredom and frustration can lead to destructive behavior or aggression, or to zooming around the house. A puppy with no good outlet, such as a sturdy chew toy, will release that pent-up energy by barking, running around, or jumping on people.

The opposite problem is just as real. Just like toddlers who throw tantrums when theyâre overtired, puppies that have too much going on can become hyperactive because they donât understand that they need a nap, and the discomfort frustrates them. Finding the balance gets easier as an owner learns a puppyâs energy levels. Plenty of activities and training sessions help, as do regular quiet times for cooling off and a quick nap to recharge.

Sources indicate that puppies learn promptly, and that includes behaviors that owners donât mean to encourage. If a puppy gets attention every time it becomes overexcited during play, even when the owner is trying to say stop, the puppy sees it as a reward, and the next time it feels neglected, hyper behavior may seem like a good way to get noticed. The fix is to interact when the puppy is gentle or relaxed, and to become less interesting when it gets overexcited, by dropping the tug toy and stepping away.

All puppies have energy, but the amount varies by breed, and a breedâs original purpose matters as much as its size. Border Collies, bred to herd sheep all day, require lots of physical and mental stimulation to keep up with their boundless energy. A more sedate breed, like the French Bulldog or King Charles Spaniel, tends to have far less energy to burn. A Border Collie puppy has less stamina than an adult, but it still has plenty of energy to manage.

Food affects everything from digestion to brain development, and it can influence sleep cycles, energy levels, and skin health. The wrong diet may contain too much of certain ingredients, often protein, which can lead to hyperactivity. Researching a puppyâs nutritional needs and checking the ingredients with a vet is worthwhile.

Sources indicate that obedience training teaches a dog how to manage its behavior, and socialization helps it get used to people, other pets, and new situations. Without them, a puppy doesnât know how to react, and a quick play session can end with an overexcited puppy that canât calm down. A tiny puppy climbing on people or nipping fingers may seem cute, but puppies donât always stay small, and an adult dog that bites or jumps can be dangerous, especially around a child or a stranger.

It has been revealed that most of the time, hyperactivity is easily corrected and comes down to diet, breed, or limited exercise. Health problems are a rare cause. If a puppy is still hyper after changes to diet, activity, and training, a vet check to rule out any health concerns is always a good idea. The earlier a problem is diagnosed, the easier it is to treat.

Puppies are still learning what their bodies are telling them. One of the most common signs is becoming hyper or restless when they need to go. An older puppy getting used to house training may be asking to go out, while a younger one may not understand the signal and burst into a case of the zoomies until it figures it out.

Most hyperactivity simply comes from being a puppy. Younger dogs are more excitable, and they need lots of energy to explore the world without yet knowing how to manage it. Puppies steadily grow out of it. They may still get the zoomies later on, but they settle and learn better control. Rewarding calm behavior, working on obedience, and giving a working breed a job to do all help.

Researching a breed before bringing a puppy home matters, since a high-energy herding breed can be too much for some households. Time matters too, because a long workday followed by evening chores may leave little room for the exercise a puppy needs.

According to recent reports, activity is the best way to manage energy, and it shouldnât be only physical. Puzzles and other mental activities keep a brain busy as well. Calm behavior deserves rewards with treats and attention, and disengaging when a puppy gets overexcited teaches that playing nicely keeps the game going longer. Training helps too, because some hyper behavior is really bad manners learned along the way, such as jumping up or racing around when the leash comes out.

Most puppies grow out of their boundless energy as they reach adulthood and learn self-control, which can take between one and two years depending on breed. Some breeds are naturally quieter and happier to laze around, while more active breeds never lose their energy. A routine tailored to a dogâs needs is essential, along with choosing a puppy that suits the family.

According to recent reports, A puppyâs energy can come from exuberance, overstimulation, tiredness, boredom, diet, or, on rare occasions, health issues. Working out which one applies, and adjusting the daily schedule to match, is the key to keeping it manageable.

Braver is a leading expert on the law of domestic use of the military and a liberal/progressive. I am a a libertarian. If we can come to agreement on these problems, I hope others can, as well. Here is the abstract:.

Emergency powers are special types of government authorities that are only supposed to be used under extraordinary circumstances, in order to address a crisis. But, over time, many have become institutionalized as near-blank checks that the executive can invoke at will. This situation imperils civil liberties and our constitutional system.

This chapter goes over the major US emergency powers, including the National Emergencies Act, the Insurrection Act, the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), and others, and offers proposals for curbing the dangers they create. Effective reform requires a combination of latest legislation and strong, nondeferential judicial review.

If Sergeant Stubby proved what an untrained stray could do in the First World War, Chips proved what a dog could do once the United States built an actual program around him. Chips became the most decorated American dog of World War II. His story also marks the moment the Army decided it should never again give such awards to an animal.

Chips was a mix of German Shepherd, Collie, and Husky, born around 1940 and raised as a family pet by Edward Wren and his family in Pleasantville, Upcoming York. In 1942, the Wrens donated Chips to the newly formed Dogs for Defense program, part of the Armyâs larger War Dog Program, formally authorized on March 13, 1942. Chips trained at the War Dog Training Center in Front Royal, Virginia, and was partnered with Private John P. Rowell. The two served in the 3rd Military Police Platoon, 30th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Infantry Division, under General George S. Patton.

According to recent reports, chips and Rowell landed in North Africa during Operation Torch in November 1942 and served through campaigns in Sicily, Italy, southern France, and the Rhineland and central European theaters. He was also present as a sentry dog at the 1943 Casablanca Conference, guarding the meeting between Winteon Churchill and Franklin D. Roosevelt.

Chips earned his fame during the Allied invasion of Sicily, Operation Husky, on the morning of July 10, 1943. As Rowell and Chips came ashore, a hidden machine gun nest opened fire and pinned down their platoon. Chips tore free of his handler and charged the position alone, seizing the gunner by the throat and forcing the crew to surrender. As a result, four Italian soldiers surrendered. That same night, Chips alerted the platoon to ten additional enemy soldiers attempting to slip through the lines under cover of darkness, leading to their capture as well.

Recent findings suggest that chips did not escape the encounter unscathed. He suffered burns around his mouth and eye and a wound to his scalp. His actions, however, swiftly became national news. Captain Edward G. Parr, the company commander, recommended Chips for the Distinguished Service Cross, citing his âcourageous action in single-handedly eliminating a dangerous machine gun nest and causing surrender of its crewâ. On November 19, 1943, Major General Lucian K. Truscott Jr. awarded Chips the Silver Star, and accounts differ slightly on whether the Distinguished Service Cross was also formally conferred or only recommended. What is well documented is that Chips also received a Purple Heart for his wounds.

It has been revealed that in 1945, Chips met General Dwight (Ike) D. Eisenhower, who bent down to pet the famous dog. Chips, true to his sentry training, nipped the generalâs hand. The incident became one of the more good-humored footnotes in his legend.

Sources indicate that washington reacted less good-humoredly to the idea of a dog receiving human military honors. After public objection to the precedent of awarding animals medals intended for soldiers, the War Department revoked Chipsâs Silver Star, Distinguished Service Cross, and Purple Heart in early 1944. His platoon nonetheless unofficially awarded him a Theater Ribbon with Arrowhead, an honor reserved for assault landings, along with eight battle stars, one for each campaign in which he served. Chips was honorably discharged on December 10, 1945, and returned to the Wren family in Pleasantville. He died a few months after returning home, from complications related to his wartime wounds.

In January 2018, more than seven decades after his service, the United Kingdomâs PDSA posthumously awarded Chips its Dickin Medal, the animal equivalent of the Victoria Cross, in a ceremony at the Churchill War Rooms in London on the 75th anniversary of the Casablanca Conference. John Wren, then 76, traveled from the United States to accept the medal on Chipsâs behalf. PDSA Director General Jan McLoughlin remarked that the honor finally allowed Chips to âtake his place in the history books as one of the most heroic dogs to serve with the US Armyâ.

Sources indicate that chips is estimated to have been one of more than 10,000 dogs who served in the American military during World War II. His story, and the controversy his medals caused, shaped military policy for decades: no American war dog would again receive an official human combat decoration, a policy that held until working dogs began receiving other forms of formal recognition much later in the twentieth century.

Industry observers note that every military working dog story, whether it unfolded in the trenches of World War I or on a patrol in Afghanistan, is also the story of a partnership. Learning that history is one of the simplest ways to honor the generations of dogs and handlers who served side by side. If these stories have moved you, there are meaningful ways to help carry them forward.

It has been revealed that support retired dogs. Not every military working dog can retire to a family couch. The Ddamien Project provides lifelong homes for retired military, contract, and law enforcement dogs whose medical or behavioral needs make typical adoption difficult.

Learn more. The Military Working Dog Heritage Museum, founded by former K9 handlers, is gathering the photographs, documents, and firsthand accounts of the dogs and people who served. Its newsletter, The Paw Print, shares many of these stories with the public.

In a recent development, keep today's working dogs strong. Canine Advancement Group, led by veterinarian Dr. Brian Farr, advocates for treating working dogs as the athletes they are, offering evidence-based guidance on fitness, welfare, and handler education.

In a recent development, follow the national tribute. The National Service Animals Monument, planned for Washington, DC, will honor service animals and their handlers across military, law enforcement, and assistance roles, including generations of military working dogs.

According to recent reports, these dogs are part of our history. By preserving their stories, honoring their service, and caring for the dogs still serving and those who have come home, we help make sure their legacy endures.

Among the dogs of the 26th Infantry Scout Dog Platoon, one German Shepherd stood out for the length and success of its combat record. Scout Dog York is credited with taking part in 148 combat missions without a single man in his patrol being killed, a record that made him one of the war's most celebrated scout dogs.

She serves as the Social Media Coordinator for both the Military Working Dog Heritage Museum and the National Service Animals Monument. When a Pet's Final Goodbye Becomes a Nightmare: The Philippines Crematorium Scandal

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1468 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dogster

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, dogster is reader-supported.
  • In a recent development, for families who have just lost a beloved pet, arranging cremation is often one of the last acts of love they can offer.
  • Sadly, for hundreds of families in the Philippines, that trust has been destroyed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, dogster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn a commission at no cost to you. Read about privacy.

In a recent development, for families who have just lost a beloved pet, arranging cremation is often one of the last acts of love they can offer. They choose a service, pay for the arrangements, and believe that their companion will be treated with dignity and respect. They may never see what happens behind the crematorium doors, but they trust that their furry family member is in caring hands.

Sadly, for hundreds of families in the Philippines, that trust has been destroyed.

Industry observers note that what began as a neighborhood concern over a foul smell quickly turned into a disturbing discovery. On October 29, 2026, residents of Barangay Minuyan in San Jose del Monte, Bulacan, were disturbed by a strong, suffocating, and foul odor coming from a nearby vacant lot. The terrible stink prompted a report and closer inspection, leading to the nightmare-worthy discovery of seven large sacks containing the remains of 26 dogs and three cats; each one wrapped in plastic bags bearing identification labels with their names and weights.

The investigation eventually led to Ahjay Paws Aftercare Pet Crematorium in Bacoor, Cavite, where many families had entrusted their deceased pets for cremation.

Recent findings suggest that by November 4, authorities had recovered 29 animal carcasses, while 20 containers of ashes surrendered by families were undergoing forensic examination. The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) is investigating possible fraud and other violations, and at least 250 pet owners have reportedly filed complaints against the organization.

Sources indicate that the questions are heartbreaking. Were these families given the ashes of their own pets? Were some animals never cremated at all? How did companions entrusted to a professional aftercare service end up in plastic bags beside a road?

For grieving pet owners, discovering that their furry family member's final arrangements may have been mishandled is an especially cruel betrayal.

Sadly, this is not the only case, or the only country, where fraud and deception have pervaded what should be a sacred service. In 2025, the Casa XibalbÃ¡ case in Quintana Roo, Mexico, exposed a similarly disturbing situation. Authorities investigating a Chetumal pet crematorium found that families had paid to have their beloved companions cremated, only to receive urns containing soil instead of their pets' ashes. Even worse, more than 180 animal carcasses were reportedly discovered during searches connected with the investigation. The case involved allegations of fraud and improper disposal of animal remains, with legal proceedings continuing into 2026.

Different countries, different businesses, but an eerily similar betrayal. And in both cases, the damage potentially reaches far beyond the families who were deceived.

Industry observers note that another disturbing side of these horrific stories is the environmental impact. Improperly discarded animal remains can create environmental hazards, particularly when several carcasses accumulate in unmanaged locations.

Recent findings suggest that as tissues decompose, bodily fluids and organic material are released. These substances can contribute to leachate, a liquid that may move through soil with rainfall and drainage. Depending on soil conditions, groundwater depth, and proximity to wells or waterways, this can create pathways for environmental contamination.

It has been revealed that biohazardous runoff, odors, and potential groundwater pollution are among the concerns associated with improperly managed animal carcasses. If investigators discover that remains were repeatedly discarded at multiple locations, removing the visible carcasses may not be enough. Surrounding soil, drainage systems, and nearby water sources may also need assessment.

The deceived pet owners deserve justice, but residents also need answers about the conditions around their homes.

In a recent development, exposed animal remains can attract scavengers, including free-roaming dogs, cats, and wildlife. Insects may also come into contact with decomposing material and potentially spread infectious agents between locations.

Not every deceased animal carries an infectious disease, and finding carcasses does not automatically mean disease will spread. However, when the cause of death is unknown, there may be no way to determine whether the remains contain infectious agents that could expose other animals.

There is another potential hazard that pet owners may not immediately consider: euthanasia medications.

In a recent development, pentobarbital, commonly used for humane euthanasia in veterinary medicine, can remain in an animal's tissues after death. Wildlife that consumes the remains of an animal euthanized with this drug can suffer secondary poisoning, with scavenging birds being particularly vulnerable.

And this is where the consequences can extend much further. Scavengers play an essential role in maintaining healthy ecosystems by removing animal carcasses before they become sources of environmental contamination and disease transmission. Vultures, for example, can consume remains that might otherwise attract other scavengers or allow infectious agents to persist in the environment. When scavenger populations decline, carcasses can remain accessible for longer, potentially increasing opportunities for pathogen transmission and disease spread.

Sources indicate that A carcass that should have been cremated could therefore become a source of danger to another animal. The irony is that the very animals helping keep ecosystems clean could be exposed to a potentially lethal drug simply because someone failed to dispose of a pet's remains responsibly.

Industry observers note that the scandals also raise questions about oversight of the pet aftercare industry. A business permit cannot demonstrate that every animal entrusted to a facility has been handled properly.

Industry observers note that families should be able to expect accountability throughout the process, from collection and identification to transportation, cremation, and the return of ashes. Records should establish which animal was received, where it was taken, and what happened to its remains.

The Philippine Animal Welfare Society (PAWS) indicates the case has also highlighted a potential legal gap. According to the organization, the alleged deception may not fall directly under the Animal Welfare Act because the animals were already deceased when entrusted to the crematorium. However, the alleged conduct may constitute âestafaâ, or fraud by deceit, under the Revised Penal Code.

Affected families have been encouraged to preserve receipts, cremation certificates, photographs, messages, and other documentation that could support their complaints.

The Casa XibalbÃ¡ case in Mexico revealed a similarly disturbing situation, with more than 180 animal carcasses reportedly discovered and families allegedly receiving urns filled with soil instead of their pets' ashes. Two countries, two scandals, and far too many grieving families betrayed by businesses they trusted.

The death of a beloved pet is already a difficult time. Families make end-of-life decisions, discuss euthanasia with their veterinarians, arrange transportation, and decide how they would like to remember their companions.

For some, receiving an urn containing their pet's ashes brings comfort. It becomes something tangible to keep beside a favorite photograph or in a special place at home. And while emotional cost is the most painful aspect for the affected pet owners, itâs also worth noting that individual cremation usually comes at a premium price; a price paid for a service not performed. But regardless of whether these pets were to have undergone individual or commingled cremation, families deserve honesty about the service they purchase.

They should never have to question whether the ashes they brought home belong to their furry family member.

There is something particularly upsetting about the possibility that an animal cherished throughout life, treated as family, and surrounded by affection could have its remains handled so carelessly.

People entrust pet aftercare providers with something deeply personal. They are saying goodbye to someone they loved. That deserves respect.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dogster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn a commission at no cost to you. Read about privacy.

Industry observers note that letâs face it: despite its somewhat complicated and controversial history, these days,Thanksgiving is built around food, which makes it one of the trickiest holidays for dogs that want to join you around the table, since many common dishes contain ingredients that are toxic to them. Some foods are fine to share in small amounts, while others can cause anything from an upset stomach to life-threatening illness. Knowing which is which makes it easy to include a dog in the day without risking an emergency.

In a recent development, turkey is safe and healthy for dogs, with a few conditions. The skin is fatty and usually coated in bastings and spices, and too much fat can lead to obesity and pancreatitis. Turkey bones can splinter and damage a dogâs mouth and digestive tract, so they should be avoided. Seasonings, including salt, can cause toxicity, so processed turkey should be skipped too. Plain meat is the safe choice, with no sauces or gravy.

Plain pumpkin is considered healthy, which is why so many dog foods contain it. Canned or fresh both work, provided the canned kind isnât pre-seasoned and nothing has been added. Pumpkin pie, with its spices and sugar, is a definite no.

Sweet potatoes are full of nutrients and vitamins, but they should be cooked and served in small amounts, without marshmallows, seasoning, or butter. Green beans offer vitamins, fiber, and manganese. They can be steamed, raw, canned, or cooked, as long as they are plain and not part of a casserole.

Corn is healthy without butter or salt, but only if it's been taken off the cob. Corn cobs are a relatively common source of intestinal blockage in dogs. Carrots, celery, and peas are fine cooked or raw and unseasoned, and carrots and celery should be cut into bite-sized pieces to prevent choking.

It has been revealed that plain cranberries are safe in moderation, though cranberry sauce and juice contain too much sugar. If they come from a dried fruit pack, only the cranberries should go to the dog. Apple slices are healthy and tasty, but the core and seeds should go in the trash. The seeds contain small amounts of cyanide that wonât harm a dog unless it eats too many, but itâs best to be cautious. The pie is for the people.

It has been revealed that cheese makes a tasty treat unless a dog is lactose intolerant, and low-fat versions suit dogs watching their weight. A small piece of plain bread is safe unless the dog has a grain allergy. It should have no raisins, seeds, or nuts, and since bread offers few nutritional benefits, it should only be an occasional snack.

In a recent development, onions are highly toxic to dogs, along with everything in the onion family, including shallots, chives, and leeks, as they can cause anemia and liver damage. Garlic should also be avoided, and garlic powder is especially potent. It can also cause anemia, among other problems, so it shouldnât be anywhere near your pet.

Stuffing is also off limits. It usually contains onion, and it often carries a large amount of butter, which makes it too fatty for a dogâs diet. Mashed potatoes are fine if completely plain, but most are made with plenty of salt, butter, and other ingredients that arenât good for dogs, so itâs best to skip them. Gravy is a problem because of its high sodium, and it usually contains onions or garlic.

Chocolate is toxic because of two chemicals, theobromine and caffeine. It can lead to death if left untreated, and the signs can appear relatively swiftly. Caffeinated drinks are risky for the same reason. Dogs are smaller and lighter than people, so it doesnât take much caffeine to cause trouble, and that rules out coffee, tea, and soft drinks.

Industry observers note that yeast-based bread dough is dangerous even though small amounts of baked bread are fine. The yeast expands in a dogâs stomach and can lead to bloat, which can progress to a life-threatening condition called gastric dilatation-volvulus. Alcohol of any kind causes poisoning in dogs, whether itâs a drink, rubbing alcohol, or hand sanitizer.

Sources indicate that A final but deadly ingredient to be aware of is the artificial sweetener, xylitol. Sometimes listed as birch sugar, even in small amounts, this seemingly minor ingredient causes severe hypoglycemia, and even if dogs survive this, irreversible liver damage can finish them off. Always keep an eye out for this one, commonly included in sugar-free mints, gums, candy, and peanut butter, to name a few.

A dog caught eating something toxic needs to go straight to a vet or the nearest emergency animal clinic. Bringing the packaging, along with a sample of whatever the dog ingested, helps the vet treat that particular substance. When itâs unclear whether something was toxic, the ASPCA Animal Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 and the Pet Poison Helpline at (855) 764-7661 can help. Both charge a fee, but they can guide the next steps and get a pet immediate help.

In a recent development, when it comes to ingested toxic ingredients, timing is everything. If you know your dog has eaten something potentially dangerous, or even if you just suspect it, donât wait for clinical signs to appear. By then, it may already be too late. Far better to pay for an overcautious detox than risk the life of a four-legged family member.

Thanksgiving can be enjoyable for the whole family, dogs included, as long as ingredients and leftovers arenât left out for a dog to gobble down. Be familiar with ingredients that are harmful to pets, particularly anything toxic. A little care with what gets shared keeps the day safe and lets everyone relax.

Virginia Needn't Help with Federal Immigration Enforcement, But Can't Interfere With It

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From today's decision in U.S. v. Virginia, by Judge Toby Heytens, joined by Judge DeAndrea Gist Benjamin:.

According to recent reports, [W]e vacate a preliminary injunction preventing the Commonwealth of Virginia from rendering unenforceable existing agreements between the Federal Government and the Commonwealth's state or local agencies "to perform [the] function[s] of a federal immigration officer" unless certain conditions are met. The Federal Government may not "command" the Commonwealth's "officers, or those of [its] political subdivisions" (Printz v. U.S. (1997)) to assist with federal immigration enforcement efforts, and the Commonwealth's supreme lawmaking body has imposed fresh limits on when its agents may agree to do so. That choice does not violate the intergovernmental immunity doctrine because it neither requires the Federal Government to do anything nor limits any private party's ability to contract with the Federal Government.

It also does not violate the Federal Constitution's Contracts Clause for two separate reasons: (1) because the existing agreements all expressly permit the non-federal party to unilaterally terminate without cause; and (2) even if they did not, the Commonwealth would have constitutionally valid justifications for imposing new terms for future cooperation in any event….

It has been revealed that [But] we affirm a preliminary injunction forbidding enforcement of a latest state law that regulates when federal employees may wear facial coverings and must display visible identification while performing their federal duties…. [J]ust as Congress may not "matter orders directly to the States," States may not issue orders directly to the Federal Government. We thus conclude the law at issue violates the intergovernmental immunity doctrine….

Our holding is limited. We reiterate that "an employee of the United States does not secure a general immunity from state law while acting in the course of his employment," and we make no effort to provide a full list of situations in which federal officers may or may not be prosecuted for violating state law.

We also emphasize that neither the Federal Government's broad authority in immigration matters, nor "the history and context for the enactment of" the Mask/Identity Law play any role in our analysis. Whether the Mask/Identity Law directly regulates the Federal Government does not depend on what motivated the Commonwealth's decision to enact the law or whether its various provisions (or the practices that prompted them) represent wise policy.

Finally, we do not address whether other legal requirements—including the Fourth Amendment—limit the permissible use of masked and otherwise-unidentified law enforcement officers….

Judge Robert King agreed with the majority as to the likely validity of Virginia's refusal to assist with immigration enforcement, but dissented as to the mask/identity statute. For the full (long) opinions, see here.

#101828. Latest Update: Fourth Circuit Upholds Virginia's Law Terminating Agreements to Help With Immigration Enforcement - but Strikes Down anti-Mask Law

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (730 w)

Latest Update: Fourth Circuit Upholds Virginia's Law Terminating Agreements to Help With Immigration Enforcement - but Strikes Down anti-Mask Law

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (730 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Reason

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In September, I wrote about the the federal district court decision striking down Virginia's latest law terminating Section 287(g) agreements, under which various state and local law enforcement agencies agree to help with federal immigration enforcement.
  • In a recent development, we vacate the preliminary injunction that bars enforcing the 287(g) Law with respect to existing agreements.
  • Later in the opinion Judge Heytens expands on why Section 287(g) termination does not violate the Contracts Clause:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In September, I wrote about the the federal district court decision striking down Virginia's latest law terminating Section 287(g) agreements, under which various state and local law enforcement agencies agree to help with federal immigration enforcement. Today, in United States v. Virginia, the US Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit reversed that decision. But, at the same time, in a 2-1 ruling, they struck down Virginia's law barring law enforcement officers (including federal ones) from wearing masks except in relatively narrowly specified circumstances. Here is an excerpt from the court's opinion (written by Judge Heytens) on the 287(g) issue:.

In a recent development, we vacate the preliminary injunction that bars enforcing the 287(g) Law with respect to existing agreements. The district court concluded the Federal Government was likely to succeed on the merits because rendering such agreements unenforceable violate both the intergovernmental immunity doctrine and the Contracts Clause. We disagree. The intergovernmental immunity doctrine does not apply because the 287(g) Law neither directly regulates the Federal Government nor prevents private parties from contracting with it…. The 287(g) Law also does not violate the Contracts Clause for two separate reasons: (1) because the existing agreements expressly permit unilateral termination by the non-federal party; and (2) even if they did not, the Commonwealth would have constitutionally valid justifications for requiring state and local officials to terminate or renegotiate any such agreements.

Later in the opinion Judge Heytens expands on why Section 287(g) termination does not violate the Contracts Clause:.

Sources indicate that we conclude the Federal Government cannot satisfy that test for two different, yet complementary, reasons. First, all the agreements covered by the district court's injunction expressly permit the Commonwealth's agents to unilaterally terminate without cause, which means the 287(g) Law does not "substantially impair" (Sveen, 584 U.S. at 819) a contractual relationship at Step 1. Second, even if the agreements did not so provide, neither the Commonwealth's agencies nor those of its localities may contract away "an essential attribute of [the Commonwealth's] sovereignty." United States Tr. Co. of N.Y. v. New Jersey, 431 U.S. 1, 23 (1977). Here, that attribute is the Commonwealth's power to decide whether and on what terms to assist with the ongoing enforcement of federal law.

It has been revealed that I largely agree. In my post on the district court decision, I offered some additional reasons why terminating these agreements doesn't violate the Contracts Clause.

The anti-mask law presents more difficult issues because - as the majority emphasizes - it directly regulates federal law enforcement officials. On the other hand, the law imposes the same constraints on state and local officers, as well, and therefore doesn't discriminate against them. On balance, I agree with Judge Robert Bruce King's dissent:.

According to recent reports, at bottom, a single ICE officer should never be able to override a duly enacted statute of the Commonwealth of Virginia in the absence of some federal law, regulation, or other valid supporting authority. Consider what purportedly conflicts with the Mask/Identity Statute. A federal statute? None. A treaty of the United States? None. A federal regulation or executive order? None. A written policy located anywhere within ICE or the Department of Homeland Security? None has been identified. What we have today is a single sentence in a Declaration asserting that individual ICE officers possess the discretion and ability to conceal their identities when they alone deem it appropriate. No supervision is at all necessary or required and the agency itself has no involvement in the ICE officer's daily decisions on whether to wear a mask. I cannot and will not accept the proposition that individualized discretion, untethered to any identifiable source of federal law, enjoys constitutional supremacy over a duly enacted statute of the Commonwealth.

As the majority recognizes, federal law enforcement officers are not generally exempt from state law while on the job. For example, they must obey state traffic laws when driving their vehicles. A valid federal law could override a conflicting state law. But here, there is no such overriding federal law, or even a regulation (though I'm not convinced the latter alone would be enough). Just the preferences of ICE agents. Those preferences are not enough to secure an exemption from state law. Federal law (when constitutionally valid) is supreme over state law. The preferences of individual federal officials or agencies are not.

#101827. Breaking: Grow Your Own Christmas Decorations – 7 Plants to Add to Your Garden for Festive Displays Year After Year

Breaking: Grow Your Own Christmas Decorations – 7 Plants to Add to Your Garden for Festive Displays Year After Year

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1741 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the holiday season is fast approaching, bringing the annual scramble for festive boughs.
  • Growing plants that can help you see in the holiday season in style can deliver dual rewards.
  • In a recent development, most of these perennial performers are resilient, adaptable, and low-maintenance once established.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the holiday season is fast approaching, bringing the annual scramble for festive boughs. wreaths, garlands, and mantelpiece greenery. But why buy store-bought greenery that will just end up in yard waste bags by January? Plastic greenery may be used again, but it doesn’t bring the same charm. Besides, there’s a far more rewarding alternative: growing your own living holiday decor outside your back door.

Growing plants that can help you see in the holiday season in style can deliver dual rewards. Through the year, these shrubs, trees, and aromatic herbs provide texture, wildlife shelter, and vibrant winter color. Come December, they supply an abundant, sustainable harvest of natural Christmas decorations in the form of lush foliage, pretty berries, and uplifting fragrance for seasonal wreaths, table runners, and gift wrapping.

In a recent development, most of these perennial performers are resilient, adaptable, and low-maintenance once established. Bring authentic seasonal beauty indoors with these gorgeous double-duty beauties. These winter garden plants add effortless elegance, joy and character to your festive displays, and generally they need very little upkeep, freeing you up to enjoy the season. Here are 7 standout plants to add to your yard for easy homegrown holiday displays you can harvest for years to come.

Sources indicate that your USDA hardiness zone has some bearing on the plants you add for clippings that can festoon your festive garland and centerpieces. In mild and transitional zones, any hardy evergreens and deciduous shrubs planted now will establish strong roots over winter while top growth rests. In colder northern regions where frost arrives early, tender herbs thrive indoors in sunny containers, ready to move outside next spring.

Most evergreen conifers, hollies, and woodland shrubs thrive in slightly acidic, humus-rich soil with reliable drainage. Meanwhile, Mediterranean herbs demand sharp grit and full sun. When planting woody shrubs in November, dig a hole twice as wide as the root ball. Backfill with native soil amended with organic compost, and water deeply to settle any air pockets before the ground freezes.

Apply a 2-inch (5cm) layer of shredded bark mulch around the base, keeping it clear of the main stem, to insulate roots against freeze-thaw cycles. I like Back to the Roots Organic Premium Wood Mulch, available from Amazon, to help lock in soil moisture and regulate soil temperature. In zones 6 and colder, verify that soil remains workable and unfrozen before planting. If hard freezes have already locked the earth, hold hardy specimens in a cold frame or pot until spring.

Sources indicate that when harvesting for holiday arrangements, never strip entire limbs or harvest heavily from young shrubs during the first two years of establishment. Instead, take selective snips evenly from around the plant. Always cut just above an outward-facing bud or lateral branch, using sharp, sanitized bypass pruners to prevent winter disease.

To keep cut greenery lush indoors, wait until you are ready to craft before harvesting, or submerge freshly cut stem ends in a bucket of cool water in an unheated garage for 24-48 hours to hydrate fully. Keep finished wreaths and garlands away from roaring fireplaces, radiators, and heating vents to prevent premature needle drop and fire hazards. Mist your arrangements lightly with water every few days. Hopefully the following plants will give you plenty of season’s greetings….

Nothing captures traditional Christmas decor like the glossy foliage and scarlet berries of American holly (Ilex opaca). Hardy across zones 5-9, this stately native evergreen provides year-round privacy and winter shelter for songbirds, before lending its iconic branches to holiday mantels and door wreaths. Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, slightly acidic soil. It can reach 15-30 feet (4.5-9m) tall, so allow ample elbow room or choose compact cultivars like Maryland Dwarf.

Sources indicate that you must plant at least one pollinating male cultivar (such as Jersey Knight) within 40 feet of berry-producing female trees (Satyr Hill or Miss Helen) to guarantee fruit set. Harvest small, 8-12-inch (20-30cm) sprigs evenly around the tree using sharp pruners. Dip stems in water overnight before wiring into garlands. Note that holly berries are toxic to pets and humans if ingested, so display out of reach of dogs and toddlers. You can buy American Holly from Nature Hills at a discount if you hurry.

Sources indicate that for winter drama, few shrubs rival winterberry holly. Unlike its evergreen cousins, this rugged native deciduous holly drops its leaves in fall to reveal bare branches densely studded with luminous, bright red berries that persist well into midwinter. Thriving across zones 3-9, winterberry (Ilex verticillata) is ideal for damp, low-lying, or poorly drained spots where most other woody ornamentals rot. It prefers full sun for maximum fruit production, as well as acidic, organic-rich soil.

Winterberry also requires male and female plants for pollination (and hence berries). Pair prolific female cultivars like Winter Red or compact Berry Poppins with a male pollinator such as Southern Gentleman or Mr. Poppins. Cut stems look magnificent in tall floor vases, outdoor porch planters, and minimalist wreaths paired with silver-blue cedar. Harvest selectively once leaves have fallen, leaving plenty of fruit for robins and cedar waxwings. If you fancy a golden variation on the classic winterberry, you can buy Yellow Winterberry Holly from Amazon.

When winter strips color from the yard, red twig dogwood (Cornus sericea) brings blazing crimson bark that looks electrifying against fresh snow. Hardy in zones 2-7, this vigorous native tolerates everything from boggy clay to average loam in full sun or light shade. Look for vibrant Cardinal or compact Arctic Fire, which stays under 4 feet (1.2m) tall and fits neatly into small suburban borders. You can currently buy Bailey Red Twigged Dogwood from Nature Hills at a staggering 40% discount.

The most dramatic bark develops on 1-2-year-old shoots, as older wood gradually turns brown. Cut out up to one third of the oldest, thickest stems down to the ground in late fall. This renewal pruning stimulates a flush of vivid fresh canes next spring, while providing structural crimson wands for your holiday decor. Weave flexible young stems into evergreen wreaths for classic contrast, or arrange upright branches in weighted urns alongside white pine and pinecones.

Junipers deliver unmistakable fragrance alongside feathery, silver-blue foliage studded with dusty, berry-like cones. Thriving in zones 3-9 depending on species, junipers range from low-spreading groundcovers (like Blue Rug) to graceful upright evergreens like Eastern red cedar (Juniperus virginiana) and blue-tinged Rocky Mountain juniper (Wichita Blue). Plant in full sun and sharp, well-drained soil. Once established, junipers are drought-tolerant and shrug off winter winds. You can get Wichita Blue Juniper from Trees for a compact holiday-friendly choice.

According to recent reports, their supple boughs are tailor-made for weaving lush garlands over doorways, shaping rustic table runners, and layering texture into mixed evergreen wreaths. When harvesting branches, prune lightly from the outer tips and never cut back into old, bare interior wood. Dunk cut sprigs in cool water for 24 hours before crafting, and wear sleeves to guard against potential skin irritation from the resinous needles.

Industry observers note that bridging the gap between holiday decor and festive feasting, here comes rosemary. Its pine-scented foliage brings instant charm to winter tablescapes and mini wreaths, especially paired with dried orange slices and cinnamon sticks. Rosemary (Salvia rosmarinus) is reliably perennial outdoors in zones 8-10, where it thrives in lean alkaline soil. If you are in zone 7 or colder, grow upright cultivars like Tuscan Blue or Arp in terracotta containers. You can buy Arp Rosemary Indoor Christmas Plants from Plant Addicts. Just remember to transition plants outside when weather permits.

Industry observers note that move pots indoors to a bright, south-facing windowsill before hard fall freezes arrive, watering sparingly only when the top two inches (5cm) of soil feel dry. Harvesting sprigs in December encourages bushy branching, but never remove more than one-third of the plant at once. Any leftover trimmings from wreath-making sessions can be used in holiday roast potatoes, focaccia, and mulled cider. Win-win!

For a modern, frosted aesthetic that elevates traditional red-and-green palettes, try silver dollar eucalyptus (Eucalyptus cinerea). Prized by floral designers for its dusty leaves and camphor aroma, this fast-growing Australian native is hardy outside in zones 8-11. In cooler climates, grow it as a chic container specimen that can come into a cool, bright sunroom or frost-free conservatory before temperatures dip below 25°F (-4°C). You can buy Silver Dollar Eucalyptus Trees from Trees with a 20% discount if you quote the code at checkout.

Sources indicate that eucalyptus demands full sun and gritty, fast-draining soil. In late fall, selectively prune back overly long, whippy shoots by up to a third. This shapes the plant before winter rest, rewarding you with supple stems for cascading garlands, mantel swags, and vase displays. Unlike conifers that eventually shed, eucalyptus dries gracefully indoors. Just let the cut stems dry before using them in arrangements, hanging them upside down in a cool, dark room for 2 weeks.

According to recent reports, eastern white pine (Pinus strobus) is quintessential holiday greenery. Instantly recognizable by its soft, feathery bundles of blue-green needles, this stately conifer thrives in zones 3-8. Plant in full sun or light shade in slightly acidic, well-drained soil. Give it generous space, too. Standard trees can soar 50-80 feet (15-24m) tall, but compact cultivars like Nana or Blue Shag suit smaller yards. You can get 30% off an American Beauties’ Eastern White Pine Trees from Nature Hills.

Industry observers note that growing white pine for holiday decor rewards patience. Allow newly planted trees 3-5 years to establish before harvesting, and never cut the central leader shoot, as it can ruin the tree's natural symmetry. When mature, snip 12-18-inch (30-45cm) lateral side tips around the lower and middle branches. You can weave its flexible stems into lush banister garlands and door wreaths, while its perfume fills the home.

Recent findings suggest that growing a holiday garden is a great way to get the most out of your plants, but it does require time and patience. Choose the right plants for your garden and help them get established strongly. Don’t rush the process and harvest too much too soon, and you’ll be rewarded with years of lush, natural décor.

#101825. Tech Report: Can You Burn Yard Waste on Your Property? Check the Rules Before You Risk a $10,000 Fine

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (952 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Can You Burn Yard Waste on Your Property? Check the Rules Before You Risk a $10,000 Fine

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (952 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, autumn leaves are the ornamental equivalent of spring flowers, nature’s fireworks show that excites and uplifts us.
  • Raking up and carting away is one way to tackle fall cleanup, but it is tedious and time-consuming.
  • Recent findings suggest that so is “burn, baby, burn” an appropriate way to deal with yard waste?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, autumn leaves are the ornamental equivalent of spring flowers, nature’s fireworks show that excites and uplifts us. We love it when the green foliage of deciduous trees turns fiery shades and – leaf by leaf – drifts gracefully down to the ground. But the next act is unfortunate: mountains of fallen leaves and other fall debris that needs to be removed from the premises.

Raking up and carting away is one way to tackle fall cleanup, but it is tedious and time-consuming. Burning is a quicker, easier alternative – one match and the deed is done. But backyard burning is subject to a complicated patchwork of state laws, municipal ordinances, seasonal fire restrictions, and air-quality regulations. A fallen-leaf bonfire can result in fines or even a criminal complaint.

Recent findings suggest that so is “burn, baby, burn” an appropriate way to deal with yard waste? I can't give a definitive yes or no, but as a former attorney, I will explain the general rules about the legality of burning yard waste and the consequences you might face if you do it wrong. It's exactly the kind of legal dilemma I cover in my Gardening Lawyer series. Here are the rules to check, along with safer alternatives for disposing of garden waste.

Recent findings suggest that when a landscape glitch has a legal component, you're unlikely to get a definitive yes-or-no answer. Instead, these problems depend on the applicable laws and ordinances. Whether you can legally burn yard waste in your backyard in the USA depends entirely on your state, county, and city ordinances, and current weather or fire-danger conditions. You’ll want to check with all of these authorities before burning, or ask a local landscape professional.

However, there are some general rules that usually apply. These give you a general idea of the restrictions that might be in place, what you can burn, whether burning is allowed, and what you can never burn.

The laws that restrict burning yard waste are far from uniform. More cities completely ban open burning of foliage all year long. These absolute prohibitions are based on community values like air quality concerns. Nobody likes to breathe smoke, and burning green waste releases icky stuff: fine particulate matter, carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides, and toxic smoke.

Industry observers note that some states or counties allow you to burn dry leaves and brush, but with seasonal restrictions. These may specify certain months that burning is allowed, or it might ban burning entirely during dry seasons or high winds.

Other areas allow burning but control the size of the material to be burned (for example, permitting only a 6x6 foot (2x2 m) pile). Some laws impose setback requirements to keep the fires a safe distance from buildings and roads. Still others restrict when, during a day, piles can be burned. These can be seen as safety restrictions.

Other possible safety mandates include requiring that all fires be supervised by an adult during the entire burn, having a source of water near the fire, like a connected garden hose, and a requirement that the fire be wet down and the ashes stirred when the burn is done.

Recent findings suggest that even if your jurisdiction allows yard waste burning, that doesn’t mean you can burn anything and everything. If the law permits you to burn yard waste, there are always restrictions on the types of materials that can be burned. Generally, a homeowner living in an “okay-to-burn” jurisdiction can only burn dry, natural vegetation from plants on your property. This will include leaves, brush, limbs, grass clippings, and clean wood.

On the negative side, you should never expect to be permitted to burn personal garbage, paper, plastics, rubber, tires, painted or treated wood, construction debris, or chemicals of any kind. These can release dangerous dioxins and furans that settle into soil and local food chains.

The consequences for the Illegal burning of yard waste depend on the applicable laws. In general, thumbing your nose at burn bans or restrictions can lead to severe financial, legal, and environmental consequences.

The possible penalties fall into distinct categories:.

Nobody wants to face these serious consequences of ignoring yard-debris burning restrictions. But you have to do something with all those leaves. What are your alternatives to burning?

If you shred fall leaves, small branches, and even grass cuttings, you can create an excellent compost. Spread this around your landscape. It will enrich your garden soil. It’s a good idea to invest in a shredder – like this Sun Joe Wood Chipper Shredder and Waste Shredding Machine – to speed up this process. You can also use shredded yard debris as eco-friendly mulch around the root area of trees and shrubs.

Victoria and David Beckham’s Bow-Trimmed Christmas Tree Proves Less Is More: Here’s How to Copy It

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bows are back and trending for Christmas 2026, as has been well and truly proven by Victoria and David Beckham.
  • Like trees, candy canes, and presents, bows are about as Christmassy as it gets.
  • Why, it’s a very simple addition, but it can often prove itself to be the finishing touch that brings the whole thing to life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bows are back and trending for Christmas 2026, as has been well and truly proven by Victoria and David Beckham.

Like trees, candy canes, and presents, bows are about as Christmassy as it gets. It’s the finishing touch on a really sparkly gift, the detail that truly brings out the beauty of a wreath or garlands, and it’s what makes a mantel look dressed for the holiday season.

On a Christmas tree, though? Why, it’s a very simple addition, but it can often prove itself to be the finishing touch that brings the whole thing to life.

Bows are popping up as the go-to Christmas tree ornament all over the place, from garden centers and social media, and it's all down to the likes of Kate Hudson and a whole host of other celebrities... including David and Victoria.

That's right; last Christmas saw the Beckhams decorate their traditional tree with golden-yellow bows rather than a massive collection of ornaments, and shared the results to Instagram.

Swipe to the second slide on the post below to check it out:.

A post shared by Victoria Beckham (@victoriabeckham).

In a recent development, the vibe? Why, classy and unique (much as you'd expect from the stylish pair). It’s also way easier to copy than it looks, but it's important to remember that there are a few places where bow-trimmed trees tend do go wrong.

Sources indicate that to help you get it right, we consulted the pros. Here's what they had to say.

When trying to recreate the Beckhams' Christmas tree, most people start with the ribbon, which is a substantial mistake.

Recent findings suggest that “Buy your lights before you buy your ribbon,” indicates Nadi Melam, founder and lead preservation artist at Florals Memories, who works with matching color to light. A golden-yellow bow can look orange once the tree is lit. “Warm light bulbs will add orange to anything they touch. Cool-white ones will remove any yellow.”.

Interior designer Irena Cara, co-founder of Nova Wrap, recommends warm white as a general rule: “Use warm white lights and place them deep in the tree. Avoid tinsel and multicolored lights as they detract from the ribbon.”.

Industry observers note that don't forget to do a test first. “Hold a strip of ribbon up to your lights before buying a full spool,” says Melam. “The wrong spool is your most expensive error.”.

The key word here is restraint, and it’s what gives a bow tree like David and Victoria Beckham's tree that expertly designed look.

“Bows look planned when you select one ribbon color and one width,” claims Melam. “You end up with too many choices if you use too many colors and widths. That’s what makes a tree look cluttered.”.

Cara adds texture to the plan: “Velvet ribbon adds a nice textured element to a tree. Grosgrain and wired satin ribbon keep their shape and can also add nice detail to the tree.” Her limit is “no more than two finishes on the tree.”.

While some Christmas trees look great with one oversized ribbon as per the above, those who want to emulate the Beckhams' Christmas tree need to get working on a few more bows than that.

Sources indicate that in fact, Cara has a number in mind: “A tree is finished with 20 to 30 bows. They should be spaced about an arm’s length apart and staggered so they don’t form a straight line across the tree.”.

Depth matters as much as spacing. “Place each bow deep within the tree, so the branches will embrace it,” says Melam. “If the bow is on the end of a branch, it will droop and move in the breeze.”.

Cara’s main warning is about scale: “Decorating too small is the biggest faux pas. Tiny ornaments and thin ribbon get lost on a large tree.”.

According to recent reports, do you ever feel completely satisfied when you decorate your Christmas tree only to get comfy on the sofa and realize you missed an entire side of it? “Look at your tree from all sides before you consider it finished,” notes Melam.

Cara agrees: “A tree without decorations in the back and bottom of the tree looks unfinished.”.

In a recent development, if the tree looks thin in places, definitely don’t make the mistake of adding more ornaments. “Add small evergreen sprigs into any gaps you see before you fill in more ornaments,” indicates Melam. “You create subtlety by making fewer design decisions and repeating those choices.”.

According to recent reports, cara is clear that she’s a designer rather than a horticulturist, but she has noticed which trees hold up well. “The branches of a Fir, such as a Fraser or Nordmann, will keep an even shape and hold the needles better.”.

Industry observers note that A bow-led tree also helps the branches. “Heavier ornaments and a lot of ornaments on the tree cause the branches to break and bend over time, so place fewer, larger, and more considered ornaments on the tree.”.

It has been revealed that if you’re trying to be budget-conscious, bows are also a great idea as they’re a lot cheaper than a full set of ornaments. “Using a large, wide ribbon to make bows is cheaper than buying ornaments,” states Cara.

Melam’s advice is to put the money where it shows: “Spend on lights and high-quality ribbon, then use what you have to finish the job.” If you grow your own, she adds, “You can also use dried clippings from your garden as filler.”.

According to recent reports, victoria and David Beckham don’t need a cluttered, crowded tree to make a big impression, and neither do you. Just pick the right lights, add a few golden ribbons, and you can get the same polished look in no time flat!

Make Your Houseplants a DIY Humidity Tray and Gift Them the Glossiest Leaves for the Holidays

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1486 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that many leafy plants we now grow as houseplants evolved in hot and humid rainforests which is why, now fall’s here and the heat’s turned on, the dry air in our homes is leading to less-than-lovely foliage.
  • In a recent development, it’s a cruel fact that it’s the plants with the biggest or boldest leaves that struggle most in the dry air of our winter-heated homes: adapting to life in a rainforest is exactly why the foliage is so fabulous in the first place.
  • So, if you want to enjoy these dramatic leaves at their best, you have to provide these houseplants with the humidity level they need to flourish.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that many leafy plants we now grow as houseplants evolved in hot and humid rainforests which is why, now fall’s here and the heat’s turned on, the dry air in our homes is leading to less-than-lovely foliage. So, if you're wondering how to keep houseplants healthy in winter so you can enjoy lush, glossy leaves, you're not alone. Thankfully, a humidity tray is the quick and easy DIY solution that will speed your houseplants back to happy in time for the holidays, and it won't cost you a dime.

In a recent development, it’s a cruel fact that it’s the plants with the biggest or boldest leaves that struggle most in the dry air of our winter-heated homes: adapting to life in a rainforest is exactly why the foliage is so fabulous in the first place. Beneath a dense forest canopy, sunlight is a precious commodity so some plants like Elephant Ear (Alocasia) grow huge leaves to catch as much light as possible. Others such as peace lilies has foliage densely packed with chlorophyll to absorb as much of the scarce light as possible, and that's what creates their intense, deep green hue. Some like Calathea have purple or red undersides to their leaves precisely so that precious light gets bounced back into the leaf.

So, if you want to enjoy these dramatic leaves at their best, you have to provide these houseplants with the humidity level they need to flourish. Any plant likely suffering from a lack of humidity at this time of the year is easy to spot, starting with any houseplants with brown leaf tips or edges, smaller or discolored leaves, or slow growth. Now, to restore these ailing houseplants to lush, glossy growth, you could treat them to a small humidifier like the Homedics Humidifier from Amazon. Or you could simply DIY a humidity tray with stuff you’ve probably already got in your backyard.

A humidity tray, also called a pebble tray, is a shallow container that’s wider than the plant pot it serves, filled with small pebbles and water. The plant pot sits on the pebbles above the water level so instead of water being pulled up into the potting soil, it evaporates into the air. The higher the heat in your home, and so the drier the air, the more water evaporates to create a humid microclimate around your houseplant.

An old plant saucer is perfect, or if you’d like something more decorative for your houseplant display, look in your kitchen cupboards for a deep plate or shallow dish. Fill this with fine gravel or small pebbles – pea gravel is perfect and you can buy bagged pea gravel pebbles from Home Depot very cheaply if you don’t have a gravel path or driveway to raid.

Then simply stand the plant pot on top of your DIY humidity tray and keep the water topped up, making sure the water level stays below the base of the pot.

Grouping your houseplants together will also help to raise the humidity. Clustering plants together creates an indoor microclimate because the water vapor that’s lost through the leaves diffuses more slowly – and this effect is amplified if even one or two of the grouped houseplants have humidity trays.

Houseplants that have evolved to live in the damp environments of rainforests and woodland are most sensitive to humidity. These common houseplants all thrive in 55-80% humidity and will benefit from a DIY pebble tray:.

If you grow any of these houseplants, then a $5 room thermometer like this from Amazon that measures humidity levels as well as temperature, and records the minimum and maximum levels in the past 24 hours, is a really useful tool. You’ll be able to see exactly what the humidity levels are and, if they’re too low, take action before the plant tells you it’s an glitch with brown leaf tips. Already made the plant a pebble tray? To raise the humidity further, simply DIY a wider one to increase the surface area of water available to evaporate.

Industry observers note that many more adaptable houseplants won’t be as dramatic about a less-than-ideal humidity level, but add a little more moisture to the air and they’ll grow faster and produce bigger leaves with a better color and shine. Making a DIY pebble tray will help all these plants to flourish:.

Sources indicate that these plants all thrive in humidity levels of 40-60%. While that's likely within the average humidity of a home in summer, it's a different story in winter. Because cold air can't hold as much water, and home heating dries it further, home moisture levels typically drop to 20-40%. While that lack of humidity isn't enough to kill these adaptable plants, it will certainly prevent them from looking their best.

Leaves with brown tips and outer edges are the most common sign that a houseplant is struggling in low humidity levels and is losing moisture from its foliage faster than the roots can replace it. All plants release water vapor from tiny pores on their leaves and, in dry air, that moisture is sucked out at a faster rate. The plant parts furthest away from the roots supplying the water are the first to run out of moisture, which is why leaf tips are the first to dry out to a crispy brown. At this time of the year, it's very common to see houseplants with long, narrow leaves like spider plants with brown leaf tips. Low humidity is also an easily-avoided reason why peace lily flowers turn brown.

Sources indicate that there are other symptoms to look out for too, such as slow growth and smaller new leaves. While many plants naturally produce aerial roots, if you spot a sudden escalation in their number, the houseplant is likely seeking more humidity. And if you find that the potting soil dries out super-rapidly after watering, too-dry air may be the cause.

Misting houseplants provide a quick fix but the spike in humidity only lasts for a very short time, whereas a humidity tray delivers constant moisture to create a more permanent microclimate. To match the humidity levels provided by a pebble tray, you’d need to mist houseplants every hour, every day, every night. Misting can also create a breeding ground for fungal and bacterial disease by leaving water sitting on foliage.

It has been revealed that in dry or arid zones like Arizona, Nevada, Latest Mexico or Colorado, your houseplants may need humidity trays topped up year-round. You’ll likely see even plants that don’t require very high air moisture levels developing brown tips, which is a sure sign that they’ll benefit from a humidity tray.

Industry observers note that at the other end of the scale, if you live in a high-humidity climate like Louisiana, Mississippi or Florida, only the houseplants that are highly dependent on humidity need a pebble tray – unless your home is equipped with an efficient air-conditioning system that dehumidifies, and dependant on your winter home-heat level, of course. Unnecessary standing water in a warm, damp home puts plants at a higher risk of pests and fungal disease.

Gifting many of your houseplants a DIY humidity tray will help them to flourish in our heated homes through fall and winter, and happy plants grow leaves that are larger and lusher, greener and glossier. Along with a cheap thermometer that displays air moisture percentages, your DIY pebble tray makes it very easy to adjust humidity levels, too. Keep the trays topped up with water for maximum humidity, and gradually reduce if needs be once your home's heat is turned off. You can even leave the trays water-free over summer if natural humidity is high enough in your climate, and let your DIY pebble saucers serve as stylish houseplant decor for a personal touch, until the heat's turned back on.

#101822. Latest Update: Which Kitchen Scraps Can You Add to Houseplant Soil? 6 You Can Try – Plus, Those You Should Avoid

Latest Update: Which Kitchen Scraps Can You Add to Houseplant Soil? 6 You Can Try – Plus, Those You Should Avoid

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1742 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every household generates a mass of organic kitchen waste, from morning coffee grounds to evening fish bones.
  • A few kitchen scraps can help a little, and some can actually help with fertilizing houseplants, once they're prepared the right way.
  • It has been revealed that the kitchen scraps I’ve rounded up here can help to supply trace minerals, organic matter, and subtle soil-structuring benefits to your potted greenery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every household generates a mass of organic kitchen waste, from morning coffee grounds to evening fish bones. Quite often, thanks to social media and online forums, we’ll hear about some novel way to use key scraps to help plants. These quirky DIY tricks can seem so compelling and easy (and also free) that it’s tempting to toss scraps straight into the potting soil around your plants.

A few kitchen scraps can help a little, and some can actually help with fertilizing houseplants, once they're prepared the right way. But that last bit is key. You need to make sure you are using the right kind of scraps, and that you have prepared them so they can be absorbed or processed well. Fail to do this, and there’s a chance that helpful impulse could result in fuzzy mold and tiny gnats.

It has been revealed that the kitchen scraps I’ve rounded up here can help to supply trace minerals, organic matter, and subtle soil-structuring benefits to your potted greenery. These scraps all need prep first, though, whether that's drying, grinding or some time in a compost pile or worm bin. If you want to unlock their gentle benefits, this is a good time to get things moving. Houseplants slow down as the days get shorter, so they don't need much extra food until spring – giving you time to turn some trash into treasure.

When it comes to the best scraps for houseplants, preparation and application are key. Never dump wet, chunky food scraps onto the soil surface, as they can trap stagnant moisture and invite houseplant pests. Instead, use one of these preparation methods: air or oven-drying, grinding into fine powder, brewing, or indoor composting with a worm bin.

Indoor composting bins don’t require lots of knowledge or experience these days, and you can pick up units that make composting a highly beneficial background activity. If you’re interested in a compact unit for indoors, the Original VermiHut System, available from Amazon, is a neat and super-easy way to turn scraps into rich, houseplant-safe worm castings. Once your scrap of choice has been treated, you can gently work small amounts into the top inch (2.5cm) of potting mix.

Prioritize pot hygiene with any scraps you do try out. Check that every container has unobstructed drainage holes and keep a close eye on treated pots for 2-3 weeks. If you spot any white fuzz, scrape it off and allow the top layer to dry. Remember that kitchen scraps are meant to be gentle supplemental boosters, not replacements for quality potting soil and a balanced seasonal feeding routine. Here are 6 scraps you can safely try with your houseplants – plus, which scraps to leave in the bin.

The buzz around coffee grounds for houseplants is mostly about nitrogen (along with trace potassium and magnesium). That nitrogen is tied up in organic matter, though, and soil microbes will need to break it down before the roots can use it. Select plain, unflavored Arabica or Robusta grounds, and avoid flavored coffees containing synthetic oils, syrups, or spices.

In a recent development, never spread damp grounds thickly over indoor soil, as they can mold and dry into a crust that repels water. Instead, spread used grounds on a baking sheet to dry, then blend a small handful (no more than 5-10% of total volume) into a fresh potting mix, or process through an indoor worm bin first. Contrary to myth, brewed grounds will not reliably acidify your potting soil, as brewing pulls a good share of the acid into your cup. For a good potting mix, buy Espoma Organic Potting Mix from Walmart.

Recent findings suggest that eggshells are mostly calcium carbonate, and plants need calcium to strengthen cell walls and support healthy fresh leaf development. But don’t toss large shell fragments into a houseplant pot. Calcium carbonate dissolves at a glacial pace, especially in neutral or alkaline potting mixes. Instead, rinse away the egg white, let shells air-dry for 48 hours, and pulverize them into a fine powder.

For grinding, use a dedicated grinder, a pestle and mortar, or a processor like the Cuisinart Mini Food Processor from Amazon, which is compact and super-fast. For a faster mineral release, soak the shell powder in a splash of mild lemon juice or vinegar for 24 hours. The mild acid reacts with the calcium carbonate to create plant-available calcium citrate. Just remember to dilute before applying. Work a light pinch into potting soil once or twice a year, skipping acid-loving plants like African violets, as the calcium can gradually raise soil pH.

In a recent development, banana peels (along with closely related plantain peels) are rich in potassium, which regulates water uptake and boosts flowering. They also contain trace phosphorus and magnesium. However, burying chunks of raw banana or plantain peel in your houseplant’s potting soil is a really bad idea. Dense, sugary peels rot sluggishly in pots, attracting fruit flies and encouraging root-rotting pathogens.

Chop banana (or plantain) peels into small pieces and process in a compost bin or worm farm until crumbly, before blending into potting mix. Alternatively, dehydrate clean peels in a low oven until crispy, grind them into a powder, and sprinkle a spoonful into the soil. While soaking peels in water for 48 hours creates a mild banana tea, it leaches only trace nutrients. If you’re looking for targeted liquid feeds, you’re better off with a balanced fertilizer such as Espoma’s Organic Indoor 2-2-2 Plant Food, available from Walmart, and adding it during spring and summer growth.

Plain, steeped tea leaves offer gentle organic matter, trace nitrogen, and mild tannic acids that subtly condition soil structure and improve moisture retention. However, you need to stick to unflavored black, green, white, or pure herbal teas like chamomile or rooibos. And make sure they are steeped without milk, sugar, or honey. Avoid heavily spiced chai blends or artificially flavored teas, as the essential oils can irritate delicate root hairs.

According to recent reports, tear open used tea bags and discard the pouch, as most tea bags contain plastic fibers. Never pile wet leaves on top of the soil, as they can encourage gnats and mold. Instead, spread the loose leaves on a paper towel until dry and lightly fork a teaspoon into the topsoil, or drop them into a worm bin. Used gently once a month in spring and summer, they give moisture-loving tropicals like ferns, calatheas, and pothos a gentle lift. If you don’t have any compost going, Home Depot carries Noble Worm Organics Worm Castings, and a little of that does the same job.

Recent findings suggest that pungent alliums like onions and garlic, spicy peppers, or fibrous potato skins should never be buried straight into pots. They can ferment and summon fungus gnats. However, you can safely capture minerals by making a liquid tonic from key vegetable scraps. Save the cooled, unsalted water left over from boiling or steaming nutrient-dense vegetables like carrots, potatoes, broccoli, or leafy greens. Use this mineral-rich water at room temperature instead of watering once or twice a month, discarding any leftovers after 24 hours so bacteria cannot multiply.

Alternatively, you can route clean trimmings through an indoor worm bin. Bury solid scraps like carrot peelings, lettuce cores, and squash trimmings beneath damp bedding in a compact indoor worm bin. In 8-12 weeks, red wigglers can convert them into odorless vermicompost. You can buy Uncle Jim’s Worm Farm Live Red Wigglers from Amazon for hardworking composting worms to transform carrot peels and used greens into nutrient-rich castings. Then add to plants, applying 2 tablespoons (30 ml) per quart (0.95 L) of potting mix around the base, and water in.

In a recent development, rinsing uncooked white, brown, or jasmine rice leaves behind cloudy, starch-rich water containing trace amounts of nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium (NPK) along with B vitamins. While scientific evidence reveals its direct fertilizer value is modest and varies widely by grain type, those gentle starches can act as a mild prebiotic snack for beneficial soil microbes in healthy potting mixes. However, use only fresh, unsalted and unseasoned rinse water (or cooled, unsalted boiling water).

Apply it the same day in place of a standard watering once a month. Never store rice water in jars to ferment. DIY fermented rice water quickly breeds foul-smelling bacteria. Likewise, avoid salted pasta water. While plain starchy pasta water is harmless, even a pinch of cooking salt accumulates in closed pots and can quickly reach a level where it scorches roots. If you’re after a good indoor watering can, choose something with a gooseneck spout that can target the base of the plant, such as the Megawodar Copper Watering Can from Amazon.

Recent findings suggest that even with careful prep, certain kitchen leftovers need to be kept far away from your indoor garden. Meat, fish, and dairy products are the substantial ones. Oily and greasy foods are also non-starters. Animal proteins and fats rot rapidly in warm indoor temperatures, creating unbearable odors, attracting flies, and coating soil particles in a waterproof film that suffocates roots.

Industry observers note that salty and sugary leftovers are equally destructive. Salted pasta water, soup broths, and seasoned cooking liquids leave behind sodium deposits that build up in closed pots, drawing moisture out of roots and leaving foliage with crispy brown leaf tips. Meanwhile, sugary sauces, fruit juices, and citrus rinds trigger fungal growth and attract household ants.

When monitoring your houseplants in the weeks after adding your kitchen scraps, keep a close eye out for fuzzy molds and fungus gnats. Used early, you can add sticky traps like LightsMax Dual-Sided Yellow Sticky Traps from The Home Depot to manage adult gnats and other flying pests.

By drying, grinding, or brewing, or letting an indoor worm bin do the heavy lifting first, you can enrich your potting mix sustainably and give your houseplants a gentle helping hand with ingredients destined for the trash.
